title: Concrete Functions in Private Simultaneous Quantum Messages: Quantum Advantages and Structural Limitations

paper.title: Concrete Functions in Private Simultaneous Quantum Messages: Quantum Advantages and Structural Limitations
paper.abstract:
Abstract Private simultaneous quantum messages (PSQM) provide a minimal model of noninteractive secure multiparty quantum computation,
yet their communication complexity for concrete functions remains poorly understood.
We show that familiar total functions already exhibit both genuine quantum advantages and strong structural limitations. For three-party equality on n n -bit inputs, which determines whether the players’ n n -bit strings are identical,
we construct an entanglement-assisted protocol with asymptotic communication ( 1.633 ​ … ) ​ n (1.633\ldots)n qubits,
whereas every perfectly correct protocol without prior entanglement requires at least 3 ​ n 3n qubits.
For three-bit majority, one shared GHZ state and one transmitted qubit per player suffice for perfect correctness and perfect privacy,
reducing the communication from the optimal classical cost of six bits to three qubits. Three-bit AND behaves differently.
No perfectly correct and perfectly private protocol exists when the players share an arbitrary three-qubit state, apply arbitrary local unitary encodings, and transmit one qubit each.
However, increasing the local dimension overcomes this obstruction: one shared three-qutrit GHZ state and one transmitted qutrit per player yield a one-shot protocol with total communication 3 ​ log 2 ​ 3 3\log_{2}3 . Together with the six-bit classical lower bound, this gives a strict quantum communication advantage. More generally, for every k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 , we construct a perfectly correct and perfectly private one-shot protocol for k k -bit AND using one qudit of dimension at most k k per player, and hence at most k ​ log 2 ​ k k\log_{2}k qubits in total.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Private simultaneous messages (PSM) [ 7 , 16 ] form a minimal model of secure multiparty computation. Several spatially separated players receive private inputs and send one message each to a referee, without interaction among the players. The referee must recover the prescribed function value while learning nothing beyond that value. In the quantum version, called private simultaneous quantum messages (PSQM), the transmitted messages may be quantum states, and the players may share prior entanglement in addition to classical randomness. Kawachi and Nishimura [ 14 ] introduced the PSQM model and demonstrated that quantum communication and prior entanglement can reduce communication under perfect correctness and perfect privacy. Their results include a factor-two separation between PSQM and PSM for a total function extending two-party equality and an exponential separation for a partial function. More recently, Girish, May, Orshansky, and Waddell [ 8 ] obtained an exponential separation for a partial function in the robust setting which allows correctness and privacy errors. These results demonstrate that genuinely quantum resources can provide substantial advantages across both perfect and approximate privacy regimes. The behavior of familiar concrete functions, however, remains much less understood. This issue already appears in the classical PSM model. General upper and lower bounds have been developed [ 7 , 3 , 2 ] , but a substantial gap between them remains. Various concrete functions have also been studied [ 7 , 16 ] , yet matching upper and lower bounds, and hence the optimal communication complexity, are known in only a few cases. Shinagawa and Nuida [ 21 ] advanced this line of research by deriving explicit lower bounds for concrete functions such as AND, majority, and equality. In particular, they determined the optimal classical PSM communication complexity for three-input majority and equality, while the precise complexity of three-input AND remained unresolved. This suggests that even among very small Boolean functions, private communication complexity may depend on structural features that are not captured by ordinary circuit complexity or by the apparent simplicity of their algebraic representations. This paper initiates a parallel investigation of perfectly correct and perfectly private PSQM protocols. Our goal is not merely to exhibit another specially designed separation, but to understand which types of concrete functions admit an advantage from prior entanglement and which structural features can obstruct efficient private quantum protocols. Our results reveal a striking contrast among Boolean functions. Entanglement provides communication savings for certain equality- and majority-type functions, whereas functions with a unique preimage, such as AND, encounter a strong obstruction when each player applies a local unitary encoding to one qubit and transmits that qubit to the referee. This contrast suggests that the complexity of a function in PSQM is not determined merely by its algebraic or computational simplicity. Rather, the sets of accepting and rejecting inputs and the effect of local input changes on the shared state play a central role. sections.heading: Three-bit majority and the local-Pauli landscape.
sections.text: We next study three-party perfectly correct and perfectly private PSQM protocols for three-bit functions in which each party has a one-bit input. Starting from the optimal classical six-bit PSM protocol for the three-bit majority MAJ 3 \operatorname{MAJ}_{3} due to Shinagawa and Nuida [ 21 ] , we obtain a three-qubit protocol for MAJ 3 \operatorname{MAJ}_{3} using one shared GHZ state, local Pauli encodings, and one transmitted qubit per player. We then compress the shared randomness to two bits while preserving the same two output-dependent density operators. A local parity twist converts this protocol into one for the three-bit equality EQ 3 \operatorname{EQ}_{3} . These protocols yield quantum communication advantages since the optimal classical communication costs of MAJ 3 \operatorname{MAJ}_{3} and EQ 3 \operatorname{EQ}_{3} are 6 6 and 3 ​ log 2 ​ 3 3\log_{2}3 bits, respectively [ 21 ] . We further construct protocols for a family of exactly 80 80 three-bit Boolean functions. These conditions describe exactly 80 Boolean functions.

sections.heading: A structural barrier for AND and unique preimage.
sections.text: Although the three-bit AND function AND 3 \operatorname{AND}_{3} may appear simpler than MAJ 3 \operatorname{MAJ}_{3} , the two functions behave very differently in our PSQM setting. Let f : { 0 , 1 } k → { 0 , 1 } f:\{0,1\}^{k}\to\{0,1\} be a function for which one of the two output values has exactly one preimage. We prove that no perfectly correct and perfectly private PSQM protocol exists in the one-qubit local-unitary model : the players share an arbitrary k k -qubit mixed state and arbitrary classical randomness, apply arbitrary local U ⁡ ( 2 ) U(2) encodings, and transmit one qubit each. The proof combines a structural property of one-qubit unitaries with rank bounds. After complementing the output if necessary, suppose that the unique input has output 1 1 . Perfect correctness gives vanishing overlaps between its received state and the states obtained by nonempty sets of input flips. For single-coordinate flips, the one-qubit structural lemma (Lemma 2.4 ) forces the corresponding relative unitaries to be Hermitian involutions up to global phase. The full family of input-flip conditions then produces 2 k − 1 2^{k}-1 mutually orthogonal pure-state components corresponding to output 0 0 in supp ⁡ ( ϱ 0 ) \operatorname{supp}(\varrho_{0}) , where ϱ 0 \varrho_{0} denotes the output-dependent state received by the referee whenever the function value is 0 0 . Hence rank ⁡ ( ϱ 0 ) ≥ 2 k − 1 \operatorname{rank}(\varrho_{0})\geq 2^{k}-1 . The resulting one-qubit structure, together with perfect privacy, confines this support to a three-dimensional local-action subspace, giving rank ⁡ ( ϱ 0 ) ≤ 3 \operatorname{rank}(\varrho_{0})\leq 3 . These bounds are incompatible for k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 . The theorem applies to all Boolean point functions, including the k k -bit AND function AND k \operatorname{AND}_{k} , and their complements. The contrast between MAJ 3 \operatorname{MAJ}_{3} and AND 3 \operatorname{AND}_{3} therefore illustrates two different roles of entanglement in PSQM: a single GHZ state yields an efficient protocol for majority, whereas no shared three-qubit state suffices for AND in the one-qubit local-unitary model.

sections.heading: One-qudit protocols for multiparty AND.
sections.text: The one-qubit obstruction is not an impossibility for PSQM itself: it can be overcome by increasing the local message dimension. We construct a one-shot PSQM protocol for AND k \operatorname{AND}_{k} using a single generalized GHZ state. A zero-sum-free construction ensures that the all-one input is distinguished from every other input, and a finite-field randomization hides which rejecting input was given. For every prime p p satisfying k ≤ 2 ​ ( p − 1 ) k\leq 2(p-1) , the protocol uses one p p -dimensional qudit per player and has communication cost k ​ log 2 ​ p k\log_{2}p . Since such a prime can always be chosen with p ≤ k p\leq k by Bertrand’s postulate, we obtain Q PSQM , ∗ ​ ( AND k ) ≤ k ​ log 2 ​ k . Q^{\mathrm{PSQM},*}(\operatorname{AND}_{k})\leq k\log_{2}k. For k = 3 k=3 , the construction gives a one-qutrit protocol with communication 3 ​ log 2 ​ 3 3\log_{2}3 . Together with the classical lower bound of 6 6 bits in [ 21 ] , this yields a strict quantum communication advantage for three-bit AND.

sections.heading: Classical private simultaneous messages for concrete functions.
sections.text: Shinagawa and Nuida [ 21 ] derived explicit upper and lower bounds for several concrete functions. Their protocols and lower bounds, including the optimal bounds for MAJ 3 \operatorname{MAJ}_{3} and EQ 3 \operatorname{EQ}_{3} , provide the principal classical comparison for our three-bit protocols. For two-input AND, the protocol of Feige, Kilian, and Naor [ 7 ] and the matching lower bound of Data, Prabhakaran, and Prabhakaran [ 6 ] establish the optimal classical communication cost of 2 ​ log 2 ​ 3 2\log_{2}3 bits.

sections.heading: Quantum versions of private simultaneous messages.
sections.text: Several quantum variants of the private simultaneous-message model have been studied. In PSQM, the model considered in this paper, the players receive classical inputs and may transmit quantum messages. In quantum private simultaneous messages (QPSM), each player may instead receive a quantum input register and transmit a quantum message to the referee. In [ 14 ] , the authors introduced PSQM and established separations between entanglement-assisted and shared-randomness-only protocols. Christensen and Popovski [ 5 ] constructed private-product protocols over prime fields using shared entanglement. Over the binary field, their protocol computes two-input AND using a shared Bell pair and one transmitted qubit from each player. Together with the classical bound above, this yields an entanglement-assisted communication advantage for AND 2 \operatorname{AND}_{2} . Our impossibility theorem contrasts this positive two-party result with the one-qubit local-unitary obstruction for AND 3 \operatorname{AND}_{3} . Allerstorfer, Buhrman, May, Speelman, and Verduyn Lunel [ 1 ] related PSQM to nonlocal quantum computation by deriving PSQM protocols from coherent function evaluation, a special case of position verification. Girish, May, Parham, and Yuen [ 9 ] showed that simultaneous quantum-message protocols with a low- T T -depth referee can be transformed into entanglement-assisted PSM protocols with classical messages and approximate privacy. In subsequent work [ 10 ] , they established general upper and lower bounds for PSM and PSQM, including correlation-cost lower bounds based on Nečiporuk’s measure and communication-matrix rank, and upper bounds based on Clifford + + T T -gates decomposition and Fourier 1 1 -norm. These works provide general constructions, resource bounds, and connections with other computation models and complexity measures. Our results are complementary in focusing on perfect correctness, perfect privacy, and the communication complexity of concrete functions. Kawachi and Nishikubo [ 13 ] introduced private quantum signal processing and obtained PSM protocols with a one-qubit quantum evaluator for symmetric Boolean functions and functions admitting efficient one-qubit programs. These protocols send classical gate descriptions and therefore operate in a different resource regime from ours.

sections.heading: Quantum decomposable randomized encodings and QPSM.
sections.text: In the classical setting, decomposable randomized encodings correspond to PSM protocols under an appropriate partition of the input. Brakerski and Yuen [ 4 ] developed a quantum analogue by introducing quantum randomized encodings and constructing a quantum decomposable randomized encoding (QDRE) for general quantum circuits. Gur, Huang, and Tang [ 11 ] subsequently established a corresponding equivalence between QDRE and QPSM for the qubit-by-qubit case: QDREs for k k -qubit inputs decomposed into individual input qubits are equivalent to k k -party QPSM protocols with one-qubit local inputs, with preservation of quantum encoding size and quantum communication. This correspondence does not directly cover our model. Their QPSM setting has quantum inputs and charges only quantum communication, whereas in our PSQM setting both classical and quantum message components contribute to the total communication cost.

sections.heading: 1.3 Organization
sections.text: Section 2 defines the PSQM model and gives the required linear-algebraic preliminaries. Section 3 proves the entanglement-assisted upper bounds for EQ k , n \operatorname{EQ}_{k,n} . Section 4 gives the PSQM protocols for MAJ 3 \operatorname{MAJ}_{3} and EQ 3 \operatorname{EQ}_{3} , the analytic construction of 80 Boolean functions, and the finite linear-programming experiment. Section 5 proves the unique-preimage impossibility theorem in the one-qubit local-unitary model. Section 6 develops the PSQM protocol for multiparty AND while Appendix A gives a three-party-specific shared-randomness compression. Section 7 discusses the resulting picture for concrete functions and open problems.

sections.text: The impossibility theorem of the preceding section is specific to one transmitted qubit per player. In this section, we show that the obstruction can be overcome by increasing the local message dimension. We first give a general quotient-label construction for AND k \operatorname{AND}_{k} . For every prime p p satisfying k ≤ 2 ​ ( p − 1 ) k\leq 2(p-1) , the construction uses one p p -dimensional qudit per player. We then specialize the protocol to k = p = 3 k=p=3 , obtaining a one-qutrit protocol for three-bit AND with communication 3 ​ log 2 ​ 3 3\log_{2}3 . sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: The communication complexity of natural functions remains much less understood in PSQM than quantum separations for specially designed functions. Our results show that familiar total functions already exhibit both genuine quantum advantages and strong structural limitations. Prior entanglement reduces communication for multiparty equality and three-bit majority. In particular, majority requires only three communicated qubits, compared with the optimal classical cost of six bits. Together with the protocols for three-bit equality and a wider family of Boolean functions, these results show that quantum advantage in PSQM is not confined to artificial promise problems. The contrast with AND shows that the structure of the function is equally important. Functions with a unique accepting or rejecting input are incompatible with perfect correctness and perfect privacy in the one-qubit local-unitary model, regardless of the shared k k -qubit state and shared randomness. This is a general structural obstruction, not a failure of a particular GHZ construction. Increasing the local dimension overcomes the obstruction. Our quotient-label construction gives one-shot protocols for multiparty AND using one qudit per player with dimension at most the number of players. For three-bit AND, one qutrit per player is sufficient, whereas one qubit per player is impossible in the local-unitary model. Thus the benefit of entanglement in PSQM is governed jointly by the structure of the function and the local dimension available to the players. Several questions remain open. First, the unique-preimage theorem is specific to unitary operations on a designated message qubit. Arbitrary local CPTP encodings, input-dependent interactions with auxiliary systems, and protocols in which each player transmits more than one qubit may evade the three-dimensional local-action bound. It remains open whether the one-shot quantum communication cost of AND 3 \operatorname{AND}_{3} can be reduced below 3 ​ log 2 ​ 3 3\log_{2}3 using asymmetric message dimensions, arbitrary local CPTP encodings, or input-dependent interactions with auxiliary systems. Equivalently, it is unknown whether the qutrit protocol is optimal among all entanglement-assisted PSQM protocols. The exact classical and quantum communication complexities of AND 3 \operatorname{AND}_{3} also remain open, although the known bounds already give a strict separation. Second, the finite GHZ–Pauli experiment leaves 176 176 functions without feasible numerical solutions. The most structured unresolved cases include EXACT 1 \operatorname{EXACT}_{1} , EXACT 2 \operatorname{EXACT}_{2} , and the affine extensions of two-edge quadratic forms such as x ​ y ⊕ x ​ z xy\oplus xz . A rigorous infeasibility proof or a direct analytic converse would turn the numerical census into a complete theorem for the restricted model. Third, the construction for EQ k , n \operatorname{EQ}_{k,n} relies on existential multicolored sum-free families and on a reduction through generalized equality. It remains open to obtain uniform and efficiently computable local maps, improve the lower-order terms, or construct direct protocols that bypass the zero-sum layer. It would also be natural to ask which other standard multiparty predicates admit comparable entanglement-assisted reductions. More generally, our results suggest a program for PSQM centered on concrete functions. Equality and majority demonstrate that prior entanglement can reduce the communication cost of familiar total functions. The contrast between majority and AND shows that changing the structure of the accepting and rejecting inputs can create a strong obstruction. A fuller understanding of quantum advantage in secure simultaneous communication will therefore require both constructive mechanisms, such as combinatorial embeddings and entangled secure sums, and structural tools that explain when privacy is incompatible with local quantum encodings.

We show that familiar total functions already exhibit both genuine quantum advantages and strong structural limitations. For three-party equality on n n -bit inputs, which determines whether the players’ n n -bit strings are identical, we construct an entanglement-assisted protocol with asymptotic communication ( 1.633 ​ … ) ​ n (1.633\ldots)n qubits, whereas every perfectly correct protocol without prior entanglement requires at least 3 ​ n 3n qubits. For three-bit majority, one shared GHZ state and one transmitted qubit per player suffice for perfect correctness and perfect privacy, reducing the communication from the optimal classical cost of six bits to three qubits. Three-bit AND behaves differently. No perfectly correct and perfectly private protocol exists when the players share an arbitrary three-qubit state, apply arbitrary local unitary encodings, and transmit one qubit each. However, increasing the local dimension overcomes this obstruction: one shared three-qutrit GHZ state and one transmitted qutrit per player yield a one-shot protocol with total communication 3 ​ log 2 ​ 3 3\log_{2}3 . Together with the six-bit classical lower bound, this gives a strict quantum communication advantage. More generally, for every k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 , we construct a perfectly correct and perfectly private one-shot protocol for k k -bit AND using one qudit of dimension at most k k per player, and hence at most k ​ log 2 ​ k k\log_{2}k qubits in total. 1 Introduction Private simultaneous messages (PSM) [ 7 , 16 ] form a minimal model of secure multiparty computation. Several spatially separated players receive private inputs and send one message each to a referee, without interaction among the players. The referee must recover the prescribed function value while learning nothing beyond that value. In the quantum version, called private simultaneous quantum messages (PSQM), the transmitted messages may be quantum states, and the players may share prior entanglement in addition to classical randomness. Kawachi and Nishimura [ 14 ] introduced the PSQM model and demonstrated that quantum communication and prior entanglement can reduce communication under perfect correctness and perfect privacy. Their results include a factor-two separation between PSQM and PSM for a total function extending two-party equality and an exponential separation for a partial function. More recently, Girish, May, Orshansky, and Waddell [ 8 ] obtained an exponential separation for a partial function in the robust setting which allows correctness and privacy errors. These results demonstrate that genuinely quantum resources can provide substantial advantages across both perfect and approximate privacy regimes. The behavior of familiar concrete functions, however, remains much less understood. This issue already appears in the classical PSM model. General upper and lower bounds have been developed [ 7 , 3 , 2 ] , but a substantial gap between them remains. Various concrete functions have also been studied [ 7 , 16 ] , yet matching upper and lower bounds, and hence the optimal communication complexity, are known in only a few cases. Shinagawa and Nuida [ 21 ] advanced this line of research by deriving explicit lower bounds for concrete functions such as AND, majority, and equality. In particular, they determined the optimal classical PSM communication complexity for three-input majority and equality, while the precise complexity of three-input AND remained unresolved. This suggests that even among very small Boolean functions, private communication complexity may depend on structural features that are not captured by ordinary circuit complexity or by the apparent simplicity of their algebraic representations. This paper initiates a parallel investigation of perfectly correct and perfectly private PSQM protocols. Our goal is not merely to exhibit another specially designed separation, but to understand which types of concrete functions admit an advantage from prior entanglement and which structural features can obstruct efficient private quantum protocols. Our results reveal a striking contrast among Boolean functions. Entanglement provides communication savings for certain equality- and majority-type functions, whereas functions with a unique preimage, such as AND, encounter a strong obstruction when each player applies a local unitary encoding to one qubit and transmits that qubit to the referee. This contrast suggests that the complexity of a function in PSQM is not determined merely by its algebraic or computational simplicity. Rather, the sets of accepting and rejecting inputs and the effect of local input changes on the shared state play a central role. Shinagawa and Nuida [ 21 ] derived explicit upper and lower bounds for several concrete functions. Their protocols and lower bounds, including the optimal bounds for MAJ 3 \operatorname{MAJ}_{3} and EQ 3 \operatorname{EQ}_{3} , provide the principal classical comparison for our three-bit protocols. For two-input AND, the protocol of Feige, Kilian, and Naor [ 7 ] and the matching lower bound of Data, Prabhakaran, and Prabhakaran [ 6 ] establish the optimal classical communication cost of 2 ​ log 2 ​ 3 2\log_{2}3 bits. Quantum versions of private simultaneous messages. Several quantum variants of the private simultaneous-message model have been studied. In PSQM, the model considered in this paper, the players receive classical inputs and may transmit quantum messages. In quantum private simultaneous messages (QPSM), each player may instead receive a quantum input register and transmit a quantum message to the referee. In [ 14 ] , the authors introduced PSQM and established separations between entanglement-assisted and shared-randomness-only protocols. Christensen and Popovski [ 5 ] constructed private-product protocols over prime fields using shared entanglement. Over the binary field, their protocol computes two-input AND using a shared Bell pair and one transmitted qubit from each player. Together with the classical bound above, this yields an entanglement-assisted communication advantage for AND 2 \operatorname{AND}_{2} . Our impossibility theorem contrasts this positive two-party result with the one-qubit local-unitary obstruction for AND 3 \operatorname{AND}_{3} . Allerstorfer, Buhrman, May, Speelman, and Verduyn Lunel [ 1 ] related PSQM to nonlocal quantum computation by deriving PSQM protocols from coherent function evaluation, a special case of position verification. Girish, May, Parham, and Yuen [ 9 ] showed that simultaneous quantum-message protocols with a low- T T -depth referee can be transformed into entanglement-assisted PSM protocols with classical messages and approximate privacy. In subsequent work [ 10 ] , they established general upper and lower bounds for PSM and PSQM, including correlation-cost lower bounds based on Nečiporuk’s measure and communication-matrix rank, and upper bounds based on Clifford + + T T -gates decomposition and Fourier 1 1 -norm. These works provide general constructions, resource bounds, and connections with other computation models and complexity measures. Our results are complementary in focusing on perfect correctness, perfect privacy, and the communication complexity of concrete functions. Kawachi and Nishikubo [ 13 ] introduced private quantum signal processing and obtained PSM protocols with a one-qubit quantum evaluator for symmetric Boolean functions and functions admitting efficient one-qubit programs. These protocols send classical gate descriptions and therefore operate in a different resource regime from ours. Quantum decomposable randomized encodings and QPSM. In the classical setting, decomposable randomized encodings correspond to PSM protocols under an appropriate partition of the input. Brakerski and Yuen [ 4 ] developed a quantum analogue by introducing quantum randomized encodings and constructing a quantum decomposable randomized encoding (QDRE) for general quantum circuits. Gur, Huang, and Tang [ 11 ] subsequently established a corresponding equivalence between QDRE and QPSM for the qubit-by-qubit case: QDREs for k k -qubit inputs decomposed into individual input qubits are equivalent to k k -party QPSM protocols with one-qubit local inputs, with preservation of quantum encoding size and quantum communication. This correspondence does not directly cover our model. Their QPSM setting has quantum inputs and charges only quantum communication, whereas in our PSQM setting both classical and quantum message components contribute to the total communication cost. 1.3 Organization Section 2 defines the PSQM model and gives the required linear-algebraic preliminaries.
